title: Abstraction
summary: Exposing what an object does while hiding how, and the levels of abstraction — method, interface, subsystem — that stack up to a whole system.

slides.markdown:
**Abstraction** means exposing what something does while hiding how it does it — a `sort()` method, a `PaymentProcessor` interface, and a whole ORM are all abstractions at different scales, each letting a caller depend on a simple contract instead of the messy implementation underneath.

This topic covers where abstraction shows up (methods, interfaces, subsystems), the mechanisms languages give you to build it, and the two failure modes that bracket it: abstracting too much, and abstracting a detail that leaks through anyway.

slides.sectionTitle: Abstraction: exposing what an object does, hiding how
slides.markdown:
**Abstraction** is deciding what a caller needs to know to use something, and hiding everything else. Calling `list.sort()` tells you exactly what you need — the list will be in order afterward — and hides which sorting algorithm ran, how it compared elements, or how much scratch memory it used.

That hiding isn't laziness; it's what makes the method usable at all. If you had to understand quicksort's partitioning logic every time you sorted a list, nobody would ever call `sort()` — the abstraction is the entire value proposition.

The test for good abstraction: could the implementation change completely (quicksort to timsort) without any caller noticing or caring? If yes, the boundary is drawn in the right place.

slides.sectionTitle: Levels of abstraction: a method name, an interface, a subsystem
slides.markdown:
Abstraction isn't one size — it stacks. A **method name** is the smallest unit: `calculateTax()` hides the tax logic behind a name a caller doesn't have to re-derive. An **interface** groups several such methods into a contract — `PaymentProcessor` hides which provider, network calls, and retry logic sit behind `charge()`. A **subsystem** hides an entire architecture — a caching layer, a database, a whole microservice — behind a boundary as simple as an HTTP endpoint or a client library call.

The same discipline applies at every level: name what the caller needs, hide the rest. A well-designed system is abstraction at every scale, from a single function up to the service boundary.

slides.sectionTitle: Abstract classes and interfaces as abstraction mechanisms
slides.markdown:
Most OOP languages give you two dedicated tools for building abstraction. An **interface** is pure contract — a list of method signatures with no implementation — so any class implementing `Shape { double area(); }` guarantees an `area()` method exists, with zero commitment to how. An **abstract class** can mix contract with partial implementation — some methods fully written, others left `abstract` for subclasses to fill in — useful when several subclasses genuinely share behavior, not just a shape.

Both exist to let calling code depend on the contract, never the concrete class — the mechanics are covered in full in the Interfaces vs Abstract Classes topic; here, the point is that both are abstraction tools, just with different amounts of shared implementation baked in.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: layers of abstraction in a real system (ORM → SQL → disk)
slides.markdown:
A single `user.save()` call in an ORM sits atop several stacked abstractions, each hiding the layer beneath it. The ORM call hides the SQL it generates (`INSERT INTO users ...`). That SQL hides the query planner's strategy and the storage engine's B-tree operations, which in turn hide the raw disk I/O actually writing bytes.

Each layer is a legitimate abstraction on its own: an application developer never needs to think about B-trees, and a storage engine author never needs to think about the ORM. The cost shows up only when something at the bottom leaks upward — see the leaky-abstraction pitfall later in this topic.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: abstraction vs encapsulation, the interview-standard distinction
slides.markdown:
This pairing gets asked constantly, and the two concepts are close enough to blur without a crisp anchor. Encapsulation is covered in full in [encapsulation](encapsulation).

| | Abstraction | Encapsulation |
|---|---|---|
| Question it answers | What does this expose, regardless of caller? | Who can touch the state, and how? |
| Mechanism | Interfaces, abstract classes, method signatures | Access modifiers (`private`), enforced invariants |
| Primary goal | Hide unnecessary complexity behind a simple contract | Protect internal state from being corrupted |
| Where it lives | The boundary between caller and callee | Inside the object, around its own fields |

**How to decide which word applies:** if you're asking "does the caller need to know how this works," that's abstraction; if you're asking "can this be set to an invalid value from outside," that's encapsulation. Most well-designed classes need both, but they're solving different problems.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: programming to an interface, not an implementation
Pitfall: over-abstracting — an interface with one implementation and no reason to exist
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Best practice is to always code to an interface, so every class should have one, even if there's only one implementation today."

**Why it's wrong:** an interface with exactly one implementation and no concrete plan for a second one adds a layer of indirection — jump-to-definition now lands on the interface, then you jump again to find the real code — while buying nothing: there's no variation to hide, since there's only one behavior. It's abstraction for its own sake, which costs readability without paying for flexibility anyone will use.

**Correct model:** introduce the interface when a second implementation is real — a second payment provider, a test double, a plugin point — not speculatively. YAGNI applies to abstraction exactly as much as it applies to features: a concrete class is easy to extract an interface from later, the moment you actually need one.

slides.sectionTitle: Why abstraction is what lets code change without ripple effects
slides.markdown:
The practical payoff of abstraction is containment: when the boundary is drawn well, a change on one side never forces a change on the other. Swap the `StripeProcessor` implementation for a faster one, or migrate from Postgres to a different engine behind a repository interface, and every caller depending on the contract keeps working unmodified.

Without that boundary, a single implementation detail change — a renamed internal field, a different query strategy — ripples outward through every place that reached past the abstraction to touch it directly, turning a local change into a codebase-wide one.

This is the real interview-relevant reason abstraction matters: it isn't about hiding code for tidiness, it's about controlling the blast radius of future changes.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: leaky abstractions — when the hidden detail leaks through anyway
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I've hidden this behind an interface, so callers never need to think about what's underneath."

**Why it's wrong:** some implementation details are impossible to fully hide because they affect behavior the caller can observe. An ORM hides SQL generation, but a `.save()` call that silently issues 500 individual `INSERT` statements in a loop (the N+1 problem) still makes the caller's page slow — the abstraction hid the *mechanism*, not the *consequence*. The caller experiences a leak: they have to understand SQL and query patterns to fix a performance bug in code that was supposed to hide exactly that.

**Correct model:** design abstractions expecting some leakage at the edges — document the parts of the underlying reality (cost, failure modes, ordering guarantees) that callers may eventually need, rather than pretending the boundary is airtight. "Leaky by degree, not by accident" is the realistic goal; a perfectly sealed abstraction over anything complex rarely survives contact with production.
